html:
The Longshan cultures were late Neolithic farming cultures of the middle and lower Yellow River in northern China, from about 3000 to 1900 BCE. They are known for walled towns and for very fine, glossy black pottery, some with walls as thin as eggshell.

The name comes from Longshan, "Dragon Mountain", in Shandong, near the site first dug in 1928 to 1931. Archaeologists now see several regional variants rather than one culture.

What changed in the Longshan period:

  • Population grew fast, and many settlements were ringed by walls of rammed earth.
  • Some centres became very large. Taosi in Shanxi had palaces and what may be an astronomical platform; Shimao in the north had stone walls.
  • Potters used the fast wheel, and some copper was worked.
  • Graves show growing differences in wealth and rank, and scapulimancy, reading cracks in burnt bones, began.

They followed the earlier Yangshao culture and traded ideas with the jade-making Liangzhu culture to the south.

Around 2000 BCE population fell sharply and most of the big settlements were abandoned, perhaps because of climate change or floods. Only the central plain around the middle Yellow River carried on, and there the Erlitou culture arose, the first Bronze Age state in China. Later Chinese tradition placed the legendary sage kings and the founding of the Xia in roughly this period, but no writing from it is known.
